title: The Sharpe Pint: Rockets, Rate Hikes, and the Illusion of Net Debt

opening_mood.text: Morning. If you went to bed on Wednesday thinking we were on the brink of World War III, only to wake up to Donald Trump declaring world peace and Elon Musk pricing a $1.77 trillion rocket company, welcome to the club. Grab a coffee—or something stronger—because today is going to be wild.

content.text: 1. SpaceX's $1.77tn IPO: We Have Liftoff, But Mind the Turbulence

Elon Musk's rocket and satellite giant has officially priced its record-shattering IPO at $135 per share, raising $75 billion at an implied valuation of $1.77 trillion. It starts trading today on the Nasdaq under the ticker SPCX. Retail demand was absolutely wild, with orders topping $100 billion, while BlackRock reportedly threw in a casual $5 billion. This is officially the largest IPO in human history, comfortably beating Saudi Aramco's $29.4 billion listing in 2019. But look under the hood: Starlink is the real cash cow here, generating $4.42 billion in operating profit on $11.39 billion in revenue in 2025, while the core space division and the xAI unit are bleeding cash.

The City angle: Not everyone is drinking the Kool-Aid. A coalition of US pension funds and state comptrollers managing over $600 billion have written to FTSE Russell and the LSEG protesting Nasdaq's fast-track rules, which could see SpaceX added to major indices in as little as 15 trading days. They are worried about passive index-trackers being forced to buy a stock where Musk controls 85% of the voting power despite owning only 42% of the equity. S&P Dow Jones has already blocked a similar fast-track rule, so the index providers are split.

What to say at work: 'If you're buying SpaceX at $135, you're not really buying a Mars mission. You're buying a global satellite broadband monopoly that is currently subsidising Elon's massive GPU-renting habit at xAI. And good luck with shareholder democracy when one bloke controls 85% of the votes.'
2. Trump's 'Iran Peace Deal' Triggers a Massive Cross-Asset Reversal

In a classic late-night plot twist, US President Donald Trump cancelled planned military strikes on Iran and claimed a breakthrough peace deal is close to being finalised. This sent shockwaves through the markets: the S&P 500 jumped 1.75%, the Nasdaq rallied 2.5%, Brent crude tumbled over 4% to a two-month low around $88/bbl, and the VIX fell back below 20. The market immediately started pricing out the massive geopolitical risk premium that has been baked into energy and equities since the Strait of Hormuz was largely closed.

The City angle: Macro and commodity desks are getting severe whiplash. If a 60-day ceasefire is signed and the Strait of Hormuz reopens without tolls, it will be a massive disinflationary shock. However, Iran's state-associated Fars news agency was quick to pour cold water on the hype, noting that Tehran hasn't actually approved the text yet and key deadlocks remain. Investors are highly skeptical after hearing 'deal soon' dozens of times over the last two months.

What to say at work: 'It's the classic Trump playbook: threaten to bomb them on Wednesday, declare world peace on Thursday, and watch the markets go wild. Until the tankers are actually moving freely through Hormuz, going short on crude is a very brave trade.'
3. Lagarde Hands Europe a Bitter Pill: First ECB Rate Hike Since 2023

The European Central Bank raised its key deposit rate by 25 basis points to 2.25%—its first rate hike since September 2023. Christine Lagarde cited persistent inflationary pressures stemming from the Middle East conflict and the ongoing closure of the Strait of Hormuz. Eurozone inflation ticked up to 3.2% in May, forcing the ECB's hand. To make matters worse, they slashed their 2026 growth forecast to a dismal 0.8% and raised their 2026 inflation forecast to 3.0%.

The City angle: The ECB is in a horrible stagflationary bind. They are hiking rates to combat supply-side energy inflation, which monetary policy can't actually fix, while simultaneously choking off an already anaemic European economy. Economists are already pricing in another hike in September, but critics argue this will do more damage to growth than it will to prices.

What to say at work: 'The ECB is terrified of repeating their 2022 mistake of being asleep at the wheel. But hiking rates into a 0.8% growth forecast because oil is expensive is like trying to put out a kitchen fire by turning off the water mains.'
4. Oracle Beats Earnings, But the $40bn AI Bar Tab Spooks Wall Street

Oracle reported stellar Q4 earnings, with cloud infrastructure revenue up 93% and a mind-boggling $523 billion backlog of future contracted revenue (Remaining Performance Obligations). Yet, the stock plummeted 11% in a single session, wiping out nearly $80 billion in market value. The culprit? Oracle announced plans to raise $40 billion in FY2027 through debt and equity to fund its massive data center buildout, on top of its existing $99.6 billion debt pile. Net capex for next year is projected to hit a staggering $70 billion.

The City angle: Unlike Big Tech hyperscalers who are sitting on mountains of cash, Oracle is funding its AI ambitions almost entirely through debt and equity issuance. Its free cash flow for FY2026 was negative $23.7 billion. Investors are starting to ask: when does this massive cash burn actually turn into bottom-line profits? The market is no longer just cheering AI capital expenditure; they are starting to ask who is paying for it.

What to say at work: 'Oracle basically showed Wall Street the most amazing AI party in history, and then handed them a $40 billion bar tab. It’s a stark reminder that building digital factories is a brutal, capital-intensive business if you don't have the cash reserves of a small nation to back it up.'
5. CoreWeave and Rocket Lab Join the Nasdaq-100 in a Massive Index Shakeup

Nasdaq announced its June quarterly rebalance, effective June 22. Out go legacy names like Charter Communications, Cognizant, and Zscaler. In come the new darlings of the tech and space sectors: AI cloud provider CoreWeave (CRWV), Rocket Lab (RKLB), Astera Labs (ALAB), Nebius Group (NBIS), and Teradyne (TER). This is a massive structural catalyst. With over $800 billion in assets tracking the Nasdaq-100, passive ETFs and index funds will be forced to buy hundreds of millions of dollars of these newly added stocks before the market opens on June 22.

The City angle: CoreWeave's inclusion comes right as it priced a massive $3.55 billion dual-currency high-yield bond deal, including the first-ever euro-denominated junk bond by a US AI infrastructure firm. It shows how these neocloud players are aggressively tapping both public equity indices and global debt markets to fund their GPU land grab, while legacy telecom and IT services are being booted to the curb.

What to say at work: 'The Nasdaq-100 is basically turning into a pure-play index for the AI and space race. Booting out a cable giant like Charter to make room for CoreWeave and Rocket Lab tells you everything you need to know about where passive capital is being forced to flow.'

content.text: The Great U-Turn: Trump, Tehran, and the $1.77 Trillion Rocket

If you went to sleep on Wednesday night thinking we were on the brink of World War III, you weren't alone. But in classic fashion, a single late-night geopolitical pivot has completely flipped the board. US President Donald Trump called off planned military strikes against Iran and claimed a peace deal to reopen the crucial Strait of Hormuz could be finalised as soon as this weekend. The result? A massive cross-asset reversal that saw oil tank, bond yields ease, and equities post their best single-day performance in two months.
Equities: The Dip-Buyers Strike Back

Wall Street staged a spectacular comeback on Thursday, recovering almost all of its recent losses. The S&P 500 jumped 1.8% to 7,394.30, the Dow leaped 1.9% (up 929.97 points to 50,848.75), and the tech-heavy Nasdaq led the charge, surging 2.5% to 25,809.66. It wasn't just a US party either; overnight, Asia went vertical, with South Korea’s KOSPI up a staggering 7.4% and the Nikkei gaining 4%.

The real juice was in the semiconductor space, which acted as a massive coiled spring ahead of today's historic SpaceX debut. The PHLX Semiconductor Index surged 7.9%—its biggest one-day jump since April 2025. Micron led the charge up 11%, AMD gained 8%, and Intel popped over 10% after a BofA upgrade. It seems the 'AI trade' has found its second wind, or at least its rocket fuel.
Commodities & FX: Crude Deflates, Gold Shines

The immediate casualty of peace talks was crude oil. Brent crude tumbled over 4% from its recent geopolitical highs, settling around $89.40 a barrel, while WTI fell to $86.69. This is a massive relief valve for global inflation expectations. If the Strait of Hormuz actually reopens, the persistent supply-side squeeze that has plagued global supply chains since the start of the war will finally ease.

In FX, the safe-haven US Dollar Index (DXY) slipped to 99.34 as risk-on sentiment took over, allowing the Pound to climb to $1.3415 and the Euro to push up to $1.1570. Meanwhile, Gold rebounded to $4,223/oz, proving that even in a risk-on world, investors still want a bit of shiny insurance.
Fixed Income & Central Banks: The Sticky Inflation Undercurrent

Here is where things get interesting for the macro desks. The bond market rally (which saw US 10-year yields ease back to 4.46%) happened despite a shockingly hot US Producer Price Index (PPI) print earlier on Thursday. May PPI came in at a blistering 1.1% MoM and 6.5% YoY—the fastest pace since late 2022. While core PPI (ex-food and energy) was a slightly cooler 0.4% MoM, the headline number is a stark reminder that inflation is incredibly sticky.

Across the pond, the European Central Bank didn't wait for Trump's weekend deal. On Thursday, the ECB raised its deposit rate by 25 basis points to 2.25%—its first hike since 2023—explicitly blaming the inflation pressures from the Iran war and the Hormuz blockade. So while equity traders are celebrating a potential ceasefire, fixed-income desks are still pricing in a ~50% chance of another Fed rate hike before the end of the year. The cross-asset read here is clear: equities are trading the immediate relief of a geopolitical de-escalation, while bonds are looking at the structural damage already done to supply chains.
The Main Event: SpaceX Touches Down on Nasdaq

All of this drama is the warm-up act for today’s main event: the public debut of Elon Musk’s SpaceX on the Nasdaq under the ticker SPCX. Late Thursday, the company officially priced its IPO at $135 per share, raising a mind-boggling $75 billion. This completely shatters Saudi Aramco’s 2019 record ($25.6 billion) to become the largest IPO in global history.

At $135 a share, SpaceX is valued at $1.77 trillion. On day one, it will list as the seventh-largest company in the US, instantly leapfrogging JPMorgan Chase, Berkshire Hathaway, and Meta. Retail demand was absolutely feral, with individual investors submitting over $100 billion in orders for the 30% of the float reserved for them. Institutional heavyweights also piled in, with BlackRock reportedly securing a $5 billion allocation.
The Watercooler Chat: Index Inclusion and the 'Price-to-Elon' Ratio

items: The Index Squeeze: Because of SpaceX's gargantuan size, major index providers like Nasdaq are fast-tracking its inclusion. This has triggered a massive backlash from pension funds and state comptrollers, who wrote to Nasdaq and FTSE Russell protesting the 'fast-track' rules. Passive funds will be forced to buy billions of dollars of SPCX on day one, regardless of valuation, creating a massive liquidity drain on the rest of the market. If you are in asset management, this is a pure supply-demand distortion play.

Is it actually an AI company? SpaceX lost $4.28 billion in Q1 2026 alone, largely driven by massive capital expenditure. But bulls aren't valuing it as a rocket company; they are valuing it as a space-based data center and AI play, especially given its integration with Musk’s xAI. JonesTrading has already dubbed this the 'Price-to-Elon' (P/E) ratio trade—valuing the vision over the cash flow.

The Trillionaire Watch: If SPCX pops today, Elon Musk (who owns 42% of the equity and controls 85% of the votes) could officially become the world's first paper trillionaire. It's a great pub stat, but the governance structure—giving one man absolute control over a $1.77T critical infrastructure asset—is going to keep ESG desks awake at night for years.

content.text: The 'Cash-Free, Debt-Free' Illusion: What Actually Counts as Net Debt?

If you’ve ever sat through an introductory corporate finance lecture, you’ll know the classic formula by heart: Equity Value = Enterprise Value – Net Debt. It’s clean, it’s simple, and it’s almost entirely useless in the real world. In actual transactions—whether you’re a private equity associate drafting a Letter of Intent (LOI) or an equity analyst trying to figure out if a public company is actually cheap—the definition of 'Net Debt' is where the real blood is spilled. Sellers love to define 'cash' as broadly as possible and 'debt' as narrowly as possible. Buyers do the exact opposite. Welcome to the EV-to-Equity bridge, where millions of pounds can vanish in a single footnote.

We’ve previously looked at how minority interests and associates distort EV. Today, we’re looking at the other side of the bridge: what actually counts as 'Net Debt' when a deal is struck on a 'cash-free, debt-free' basis. In theory, the buyer acquires the operating business, the seller keeps the cash, and the seller pays off the bank loans. But when the due diligence teams (usually a small army of forensic accountants) turn up, they aren't just looking at bank statements. They are hunting for 'debt-like items'—obligations that aren't technically bank debt but will require future cash outflows—and 'trapped cash' that can't actually be used to pay down debt.
A Pub-Sized Example

Let’s say you’re buying a classic City pub, The Yield & Anchor, for an agreed Enterprise Value (the value of the operations) of £2,000,000. The balance sheet shows £100,000 of cash in the till and a £500,000 bank loan. The naive calculation says the Equity Value (what you actually pay the owner) is £2,000,000 (EV) – £500,000 (Debt) + £100,000 (Cash) = £1,600,000. But then you do some digging:

items: The £100,000 in 'cash' includes £40,000 of customer deposits for Christmas parties next year. You will have to buy the beer and pay the staff to host those parties, so that cash isn't 'excess'—it's deferred revenue.
Another £10,000 of the cash is held in a restricted escrow account as a deposit for the landlord.
The pub has £30,000 of accrued but unpaid staff bonuses and holiday pay.
There is £50,000 of lease liabilities for the commercial kitchen equipment (IFRS 16 / ASC 842).
The cellar roof is leaking, and there is a signed contract for £20,000 of urgent repairs (accrued capex).

content.text: Suddenly, your adjusted bridge looks very different. Your 'cash-like' items drop from £100,000 to £50,000 (excluding the Christmas deposits and the landlord escrow). Your 'debt-like' items balloon from £500,000 to £600,000 (adding the bonuses, lease liabilities, and accrued capex). Your real Equity Value is now £2,000,000 – £600,000 + £50,000 = £1,450,000. You just saved £150,000, and the seller is currently crying into their warm IPA.
Why It Matters in Asset Management and Finance

In Private Equity and M&A, this is where deals are won or lost. The 'headline' multiple is for the press release; the net debt definition in the Sale and Purchase Agreement (SPA) is what determines how much cash actually leaves the buyer's bank account. In public markets, relying on automated data aggregators to calculate Net Debt can lead to massive valuation errors. If a company has massive off-balance-sheet liabilities, underfunded pension schemes, or significant 'trapped cash' in foreign jurisdictions with high repatriation taxes, its true Enterprise Value might be much higher than the screens suggest. This is how 'cheap' value stocks turn out to be highly leveraged value traps.
Common Beginner Mistakes

items: Treating all balance sheet cash as equal: Cash held in a foreign subsidiary subject to capital controls or cash needed for daily operations (minimum cash) should not be added back at 100% face value.

Confusing Working Capital with Debt-like items: If an unpaid bill is classified as a 'debt-like item', it reduces the purchase price dollar-for-dollar. If it's left in 'working capital', it's subject to a working capital peg and might not result in a direct reduction. Buyers will fight to classify liabilities as debt-like, while sellers want them in working capital.

content.text: How to Ace This in an Interview

If an interviewer asks: 'Walk me from Enterprise Value to Equity Value,' do not just rattle off the textbook formula. Give them the practitioner's answer: 'The textbook bridge is EV minus debt plus cash. But in a real transaction, the devil is in the definitions. I would look closely at what is classified as cash-like and debt-like. For cash, I'd exclude restricted cash, customer deposits, and trapped cash in foreign jurisdictions. For debt, I'd adjust for debt-like items such as lease liabilities under IFRS 16, unfunded pension obligations, deferred consideration from past acquisitions, and accrued pre-closing bonuses or tax liabilities. This is where the actual purchase price is negotiated.'
Over-the-Pint Discussion Points

items: "Before we underwrite this target’s multiple, have we actually looked at their cash bucket? If half of it is tied up in landlord escrows or trapped overseas, our EV-to-equity bridge is going to look very different."

"They are claiming a 2.5x net leverage ratio, but if you capitalise their off-balance-sheet commitments and add back the deferred tax liabilities, they are closer to 4.0x. The credit agreement is going to be tight."

sections.title: Quant / AI Finance Idea of the Day

content.text: The Problem with "Predict-then-Sort"

If you have ever built a cross-sectional systematic strategy—whether it is momentum, value, or a multi-factor equity model—you know the drill. You train a model (like a neural network or a linear regression) to predict next-period returns for a universe of stocks. Once you have those predicted returns, you sort them, go long the top decile, and short the bottom decile. This is the classic "predict-then-sort" pipeline.

But there is a massive structural flaw here. Standard regression models are trained using Mean Squared Error (MSE), which cares about absolute returns. In a cross-sectional strategy, however, you do not actually care if your model predicts a stock's return is 2% or 3%. You only care if Stock A's return will be higher than Stock B's return. Pointwise MSE is a sub-optimal proxy for relative ranking. Worse still, the standard sorting operator (like argsort or rank) is a step function. Its mathematical derivative is zero almost everywhere, meaning it is completely non-differentiable. You cannot backpropagate through a sort. This means you cannot train your neural network to directly optimise the rank-based metrics—like Spearman's Rank Correlation or the Information Coefficient (IC)—that actually dictate your portfolio's PnL.
Enter Differentiable Sorting (Torchsort)

To bridge this gap, machine learning researchers introduced "differentiable sorting and ranking". Instead of using a hard sorting operator, we use a continuous relaxation. In their seminal ICML 2020 paper, Mathieu Blondel and his co-authors showed that sorting can be formulated as a projection onto a permutahedron, which can be solved efficiently using isotonic regression. This mathematical trick gives us a "soft rank" operator that is fully differentiable.

By swapping standard sorting for a soft rank layer (using libraries like torchsort), your neural network can output raw alpha scores, softly rank them, and then compute a loss function directly on those soft ranks. This allows you to train your model end-to-end to directly maximise the Spearman correlation between your predicted ranks and the actual future returns. The gradients flow smoothly all the way back to your input features, forcing the model to learn how to rank, rather than how to predict absolute numbers.
A Quick PyTorch Example

import torch
import torchsort

# Simulated model predictions and actual future returns for 5 assets
pred_scores = torch.tensor([[1.2, 5.4, -0.5, 3.1, 2.0]], requires_grad=True)
true_returns = torch.tensor([[0.02, 0.08, -0.01, 0.05, 0.03]])

# Compute soft ranks (regularisation_strength controls the smoothness)
# A higher value makes it smoother (more differentiable but less accurate)
pred_ranks = torchsort.soft_rank(pred_scores, regularization_strength=0.1)
true_ranks = torchsort.soft_rank(true_returns, regularization_strength=0.1)

# Compute a differentiable Spearman correlation loss
pred_mean = pred_ranks.mean()
true_mean = true_ranks.mean()
nom = ((pred_ranks - pred_mean) * (true_ranks - true_mean)).sum()
denom = torch.sqrt(((pred_ranks - pred_mean)**2).sum() * ((true_ranks - true_mean)**2).sum())
spearman_corr = nom / denom

# Minimise negative correlation to maximise actual correlation
loss = -spearman_corr
loss.backward()

print("Gradients for pred_scores:", pred_scores.grad)
The Paper Angle

In their paper "Building Cross-Sectional Systematic Strategies by Learning to Rank", Daniel Poh and his co-authors at the Oxford Man Institute applied learning-to-rank algorithms to cross-sectional momentum strategies. They demonstrated that moving away from pointwise regression and instead training models to learn pairwise and listwise structures across instruments led to a massive boost in trading performance—providing up to a threefold increase in Sharpe ratios compared to traditional approaches. By directly aligning the model's training objective with the portfolio's ranking-based execution, they eliminated the "predict-then-sort" mismatch.
The Pub / Interview Conversation Starter

The next time a colleague or an interview candidate brags about their deep learning model predicting asset returns with a low MSE, ask them this: "Why are you optimising for absolute return errors when your execution strategy only cares about relative cross-sectional ranking? Why not use a differentiable sorting layer like Torchsort to directly optimise the Spearman correlation of your portfolio?" It is a brilliant way to show you understand the critical link between machine learning loss functions and real-world portfolio construction.

sections.title: One Article or Paper Worth Reading

content.text: What Investment Data Implies about the AI Transition by Jessica Wachter (Wharton) and Jonathan Wachter (Point72). NBER Working Paper No. 35290 (June 2026).
Why this one?

Most AI commentary falls into two equally annoying camps: the techno-utopians who think we will all be uploaded to the cloud by next Thursday, and the cynical bears who scream bubble every time Nvidia ticks down. This paper is different. Written by a top Wharton finance professor and a Point72 researcher, it bypasses the hand-waving and uses hard capital expenditure data to reverse-engineer exactly what the market is betting on. It treats the massive capex of the hyperscalers not as a tech story, but as a giant, leveraged macroeconomic gamble.
The Detailed Breakdown

Let us start with the sheer scale of the cash being burned. The five largest US tech firms spent 380 billion dollars on capex in 2025 and are on track to spend roughly double that in 2026, scaling from 155 billion dollars in 2022 to a projected 755 billion dollars in 2026. As the authors bluntly point out, these firms are betting the ranch. If these investments do not yield massive, unprecedented profits, they face genuine insolvency risk. To justify this spend on a Net Present Value (NPV) basis, the authors' model shows that a rare productivity boom must occur, raising AI-sector productivity by a factor of roughly 2.7x.
The paper models a two-year window where there is a 50% annual probability of this 2.7x productivity boom materialising, leading to three potential macro paths by 2030:

items: The Moderate Scenario (one boom only): AI adds about 5 percentage points to cumulative US GDP growth over a seven-year transition, on top of the 19% baseline growth.
The Transformative Scenario (one further boom): AI adds a massive 20 percentage points to cumulative GDP growth.
The Singularity Scenario (two additional booms): AI adds over 58 percentage points to cumulative GDP growth, with the AI sector growing to make up between 8% and 39% of the entire economy.

content.text: But here is the kicker for markets: this transition is not free. Because of the massive investment demand and expected future growth, the model predicts that standard investor preferences (risk aversion of 3) will push the risk-free rate up by about 50 basis points. More importantly, because the risk of the boom failing is so binary and catastrophic for the hyperscalers, the equity risk premium rises by a whopping 300 basis points. In other words, the AI transition makes the risk-free rate higher and the stock market a hell of a lot riskier.
Key Takeaways

items: The Capex Implies a 2.7x Multiplier: Big Tech's spending only makes financial sense if the AI-exposed sectors experience a near-tripling of productivity.
Macro Rates are Going Up: The sheer demand for capital to fund this transition puts structural upward pressure on r* (the natural rate of interest).
The Equity Premium Must Widen: The binary nature of the AI bet—either we get a productivity miracle or a massive tech-debt bust—means investors demand a much higher premium to hold equities.

content.text: Choice Quotes

The five largest U.S. technology firms spent $380 billion on capital expenditure in 2025 and are forecast to spend roughly double that in 2026. These firms risk bankruptcy unless expected profits grow commensurately.
Calibrating the boom size to match the observed investment ramp implies that each boom raises AI-sector productivity by a factor of roughly 2.7.
What to Skim vs. What to Read

Skim the heavy math of the two-sector open-economy general equilibrium model and the stochastic calculus proofs in the appendix unless you are a glutton for punishment. Focus your energy on Section 4 (the calibration to actual tech capex) and Section 5 (the asset pricing and macro implications). That is where the commercial gold is.
How it Connects to You

If you are in asset management, equity research, or macro strategy, this paper provides a rigorous framework to explain why tech valuations are so high while the broader equity risk premium remains under pressure. It also gives you a solid, data-backed argument for why interest rates might stay structurally higher for longer, independent of short-term central bank inflation-fighting.
What to Say Over a Pint

Instead of debating whether AI is a bubble over beers, look at the Wachter & Wachter paper. They showed that Big Tech's capex implies we need a 2.7x productivity jump in the AI sector just to break even on an NPV basis. If we do not get it, the insolvency risk is systemic. That binary bet is exactly why the equity risk premium has to widen by 300 basis points to compensate for the tail risk.
Our Take

This is a brilliant piece of reverse-engineering. It proves that the AI bubble is not just a speculative mania driven by retail FOMO; it is a massive, institutional capital allocation bet being run on the balance sheets of five corporate giants. If they are right, we are looking at a 7% long-term annual GDP growth rate. If they are wrong, the write-downs will be historic. It is the ultimate high-stakes game of macro poker, and we are all sitting at the table.

content.text: The Ringelmann Effect (or why giant project teams produce rubbish)

Ever noticed how a tight team of three can pull together a brilliant, airtight pitch deck in 48 hours, while a cross-functional steering committee of fifteen takes three weeks to produce a bloated, error-strewn PowerPoint deck that says absolutely nothing? There is a proper psychological reason for this, and it is called the Ringelmann Effect (often referred to as social loafing).

Back in 1913, a French agricultural engineer named Maximilien Ringelmann conducted a simple experiment. He asked people to pull on a rope, first individually, and then in groups. You would think that if one person can pull 100kg of force, two people would pull 200kg, and eight would pull 800kg. Not even close. Ringelmann found that when two people pulled together, they only exerted about 93% of their individual capacity. By the time he got to a group of eight, individual effort plummeted to just 49%. The total force of eight people pulling together was less than four people pulling individually.

This drop-off happens for two main reasons: coordination loss (people literally getting in each other's way) and motivation loss (the psychological safety of hiding in a crowd, also known as the diffusion of responsibility).
Why it matters in the City

In finance, we love throwing resources at problems. If a deal is going sideways or a client presentation is high-stakes, the instinct is to get more bodies on it. But in reality, adding more people to a working group often dilutes individual accountability to near-zero. Take the classic investment banking pitch-book prep. When a deal team has two analysts, an associate, and an MD, everyone knows exactly what they need to do. But when you expand that to include three different product groups, a sector specialist, and a couple of advisory directors, the Ringelmann Effect kicks in hard.

Everyone assumes someone else is double-checking the DCF assumptions on slide 14, or that the sector team has verified the market-share data. Because responsibility is diffused across a massive email chain, the final product is often a disjointed, Frankenstein-like deck where nobody actually owns the narrative. The same thing happens in giant investment committees. If you have twelve people in the room, the incentive to do deep, independent due diligence drops because each person's individual accountability is diluted to 1/12th. It is much easier to nod along and assume the lead analyst did the heavy lifting.
How to use this at work

items: Enforce the Two-Pizza Rule: Keep your working groups small enough to be fed by two pizzas (usually 5 to 8 people). If a meeting has more than 8 people, it is no longer a working session—it is a performance.

Assign names, not teams: Never leave a task assigned to the team or the analyst pool. If a slide needs doing, assign it to a specific person. When someone's name is next to a deliverable, the Ringelmann Effect vanishes.

Call out specific contributions: In meetings, do not throw out a generic 'any comments on the model?' to a room of ten people. You will get blank stares. Instead, ask directly: 'Tom, you looked at the cash flow projections—do those growth rates look realistic to you?'

content.text: One line to remember
If everyone is responsible, then nobody is.
